# The Role of Hard Core Repulsion in Hyperonic Neutron Stars

This study investigates the influence of hard core repulsion in the baryon-baryon interaction at short distances on the fundamental properties of neutron stars, with particular emphasis on the structural and mass characteristics that emerge from this microphysical input. The interaction between baryons at very short separations is a critical component of the nuclear equation of state (EoS), and understanding how repulsive core effects propagate to macroscopic stellar properties represents an important theoretical challenge in nuclear astrophysics.

The research specifically focuses on scenarios in which hyperons—strange baryons such as the Λ, Σ, and Ξ particles—are present within the dense interior of a neutron star. The appearance of hyperons is expected to occur once the central density of the star exceeds a few times nuclear saturation density, as it becomes energetically favorable for the system to convert energetic neutrons into hyperons via weak interactions. This process, while thermodynamically favorable, has long been recognized as introducing significant softening of the equation of state, since hyperons open new degrees of freedom that reduce the degeneracy pressure at a given density.

A central finding of this work is that the inclusion of hard core repulsion in the baryon-baryon interaction allows neutron star masses to reach values as large as approximately 2 solar masses, even when hyperonic degrees of freedom are present in the stellar core. This is a particularly significant result because it directly addresses what is commonly known as the "hyperon puzzle" in neutron star physics—the apparent tension between the softening of the EoS due to hyperon appearance and the observational requirement that neutron stars can attain masses close to or exceeding two solar masses, as confirmed by precise measurements of several pulsars.

This finding demonstrates that hyperon-containing neutron stars are not necessarily precluded from achieving high masses, contrary to what simpler treatments of the hyperonic EoS might suggest. The softening effect traditionally associated with hyperon degrees of freedom can be substantially counteracted by the additional pressure support provided by strong short-range repulsive forces between baryons. This repulsive component becomes increasingly important at the high densities characteristic of neutron star cores, where baryons are forced into close proximity and the details of the short-distance interaction potential become dynamically significant.

Taken together, these results suggest that short-distance repulsive interactions between baryons play a crucial and previously underappreciated role in supporting massive neutron stars, even in the presence of hyperonic degrees of freedom. This underscores the importance of accurately modeling the hard core structure of the baryon-baryon interaction when constructing realistic equations of state for dense matter, and it offers a promising avenue for reconciling hyperon-admixed neutron star models with current astrophysical mass constraints. These findings have broader implications for our understanding of the composition and structure of matter in the extreme densities found in neutron star interiors.

# The Role of Short-Range Repulsion in Baryon-Baryon Interactions and Its Impact on Neutron Star Properties

## Introduction

Neutron stars represent one of the most extreme laboratories for testing our understanding of dense matter physics. Their interiors, particularly the cores, can reach densities several times that of normal nuclear matter, creating conditions where the fundamental degrees of freedom of matter may include not only nucleons but also strange baryons known as hyperons (Λ, Σ, and Ξ particles). The presence of hyperons in neutron star matter has long been recognized as thermodynamically favorable once the nucleon chemical potential becomes large enough to make hyperon production energetically possible, typically at densities of 2-3 times nuclear saturation density.

## The Hyperon Puzzle

The appearance of hyperons in dense matter has historically presented a significant theoretical challenge known as the "hyperon puzzle." When hyperons appear in the equation of state (EoS) of neutron star matter, they generally soften the EoS considerably. This softening occurs because hyperons provide additional degrees of freedom that can accommodate the Pauli exclusion principle's pressure buildup at high density, effectively reducing the pressure support against gravitational collapse at a given density.

This softening effect becomes particularly problematic when confronted with observational data. The discovery of neutron stars with masses close to or exceeding 2 solar masses—such as PSR J0348+0432 and PSR J0740+6620—placed stringent constraints on the neutron star equation of state. Traditional hyperonic equations of state, which typically only incorporate attractive interactions between hyperons and nucleons calibrated to hypernuclear data, generally predict maximum neutron star masses significantly below these observational thresholds, often around 1.4-1.6 solar masses. This created an apparent contradiction: hyperons should appear based on chemical equilibrium arguments, yet their presence seems incompatible with the existence of massive neutron stars.

## The Role of Short-Range Repulsion

This study addresses this puzzle by examining a crucial but often underappreciated aspect of the baryon-baryon interaction: the hard-core repulsive component that manifests at very short distances between baryons. In nucleon-nucleon interactions, this repulsive core is well-established and plays a critical role in providing the stiffness necessary to support massive neutron stars even in purely nucleonic matter.

The analysis extends this concept to the hyperon sector, investigating how repulsive core interactions in the baryon-baryon channel—including hyperon-nucleon (YN) and hyperon-hyperon (YY) interactions—affect the overall stiffness of the equation of state when hyperons are present. Unlike previous treatments that focused primarily on the attractive components of these interactions (which are more directly constrained by the limited hypernuclear data available), this work systematically incorporates repulsive short-range effects that become increasingly important at the high densities relevant to neutron star cores.

## Methodology

The theoretical framework employed combines microscopic baryon-baryon interaction models, potentially derived from meson-exchange or chiral effective field theory approaches, with many-body techniques for computing neutron star matter properties. These calculations typically account for:

1. The full baryon octet (n, p, Λ, Σ⁻, Σ⁰, Σ⁺, Ξ⁻, Ξ⁰) with appropriate coupling to the meson fields
2. Density-dependent repulsive interactions that become dominant at short distances between baryons
3. Charge neutrality and beta equilibrium conditions appropriate for neutron star matter
4. Solutions to the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff (TOV) equations to derive mass-radius relationships

By systematically varying the strength of the repulsive core parameters within the constraints allowed by available hypernuclear data, the study explores how this previously underexplored interaction channel affects the maximum mass achievable.

## Key Findings

The central result of this analysis demonstrates that when hard-core repulsion is properly incorporated into the hyperon-nucleon and hyperon-hyperon interaction channels, the equation of state can be sufficiently stiff to support neutron stars with masses reaching approximately 2 solar masses, even with a substantial hyperon population in the core.

This finding represents a significant departure from earlier hyperonic equation of state calculations that predominantly employed attractive-only interactions. The repulsive core effectively counteracts the softening tendency typically associated with hyperon appearance, providing the additional pressure support needed at high densities to sustain massive neutron star configurations.

## Resolution of the Hyperon Puzzle

This result offers a compelling resolution to the hyperon puzzle without requiring exotic solutions previously proposed in the literature, such as:
- Complete suppression of hyperon appearance through strongly repulsive hyperonic mean fields
- Phase transitions to quark matter that would bypass hyperonic degrees of freedom
- Modified gravity theories or alternative descriptions of dense matter

Instead, the solution lies within a more complete and realistic treatment of the baryon-baryon interaction itself, specifically acknowledging that the same physical principles governing repulsive cores in nucleon-nucleon interactions should logically extend to interactions involving strange baryons.

## Implications and Significance

These findings have important implications for our understanding of neutron star interiors and the broader field of dense matter physics:

1. **Consistency of hyperon appearance**: The results support the physical expectation that hyperons should appear in neutron star matter at sufficiently high densities, consistent with basic thermodynamic principles, without requiring this to conflict with mass observations.

2. **Equation of state constraints**: The work provides new constraints on the hyperonic sector of the equation of state, suggesting that repulsive core parameters, alongside attractive well depths, should be considered when calibrating hyperon-nucleon interactions to both hypernuclear and astrophysical data.

3. **Compact star composition**: The findings suggest that the cores of the most massive observed neutron stars may indeed contain significant hyperon populations, contrary to interpretations that used the 2-solar-mass constraint to argue against strangeness-bearing matter in these objects.

4. **Nuclear physics connections**: This work strengthens the connection between terrestrial nuclear physics experiments (which constrain baryon-baryon interactions) and astrophysical observations, demonstrating how improved microscopic interaction models can resolve apparent contradictions between different physical regimes.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates that the long-standing hyperon puzzle in neutron star physics can be substantially alleviated through more careful treatment of the short-range repulsive components in baryon-baryon interactions. By incorporating hard-core repulsion effects that parallel those well-established in nucleon-nucleon interactions, hyperonic equations of state can achieve sufficient stiffness to support neutron stars with masses around 2 solar masses. This finding reconciles the thermodynamic expectation that hyperons should populate neutron star cores at high density with the observational reality of massive neutron stars, offering a more unified and physically consistent picture of dense baryonic matter under extreme astrophysical conditions.

counterfactuals.output:
# Abstract

The equation of state (EOS) of dense baryonic matter remains one of the central open problems in nuclear astrophysics, particularly regarding the role of hyperons in neutron star (NS) interiors. While the appearance of hyperons at supranuclear densities is thermodynamically favored, it typically leads to a substantial softening of the EOS, producing maximum NS masses inconsistent with the ~2 solar mass pulsars observed to date—the well-known "hyperon puzzle." In this work, we investigate the impact of short-range, hard-core repulsion in the baryon-baryon interaction on the resulting EOS and global NS properties. Using a relativistic mean-field framework extended to include the full baryon octet, we systematically vary the strength and range of repulsive vector-meson couplings in the hyperonic channels, motivated by quark-model and lattice QCD constraints on short-distance baryon-baryon dynamics. We find that sufficiently strong hard-core repulsion among hyperons, and between hyperons and nucleons, stiffens the high-density EOS enough to support maximum masses compatible with $2\,M_\odot$ pulsars while still allowing hyperons to appear at a few times nuclear saturation density. We compute mass-radius relations, tidal deformabilities, and particle compositions, and compare our results with multimessenger constraints from NICER and gravitational-wave observations of binary NS mergers (GW170817, GW190425). Our results indicate that repulsive core effects, rather than the suppression of hyperon onset, may resolve the hyperon puzzle, and we discuss implications for the underlying baryon-baryon interaction models and future observational tests.

# Summary: Repulsive Hyperon Interactions and 2-Solar-Mass Neutron Stars

## The Problem: The "Hyperon Puzzle"

Neutron stars are extremely dense objects where matter reaches densities several times that found in atomic nuclei. At such densities, standard nuclear physics predicts that hyperons (baryons containing strange quarks, such as Λ and Σ particles) should appear, since converting neutrons into hyperons becomes energetically favorable once neutron chemical potentials get large enough.

This creates a well-known tension: when hyperons appear, they typically soften the equation of state (EoS)—meaning pressure increases more slowly with density—because hyperons provide additional low-momentum states that relieve the degeneracy pressure of neutrons. A softer EoS generally cannot support very massive stars, yet observations have confirmed neutron stars with masses close to **2 solar masses** (e.g., PSR J0348+0432, PSR J1614-2230). This conflict is the "hyperon puzzle": hyperons should be present but seem incompatible with the heaviest observed neutron stars.

## Key Idea: Short-Range Repulsion

The resolution explored in this line of research is that the baryon-baryon interaction, particularly among hyperons and between hyperons and nucleons, includes **strong short-range repulsive components**, analogous to but modified from the well-established repulsive core in nucleon-nucleon forces.

This repulsion is often modeled through:
- **Vector meson exchange** (ω, φ mesons) in relativistic mean-field (RMF) frameworks, where hyperon-hyperon and hyperon-nucleon repulsion is enhanced via SU(6) or SU(3) flavor symmetry relations applied to the vector coupling constants.
- **Multi-body repulsive forces** (three-body forces analogous to those needed in pure nucleonic matter), which become increasingly important at high density.
- **Quark Pauli blocking effects**, sometimes invoked as a physical origin for short-range repulsion between octet baryons at very short distances, since baryons begin to overlap and quark substructure matters.

## Mechanism for Stiffening the EoS

The repulsive short-range force acts primarily at high density (where baryons are close together), while having a comparatively small effect at nuclear saturation density where hyperon interaction parameters are constrained by hypernuclear data (Λ binding energies in single- and double-Λ hypernuclei).

This allows the models to:
1. Remain consistent with **empirical hypernuclear physics** at moderate densities.
2. Provide substantially **increased pressure at supra-nuclear densities**, which counteracts the softening caused by hyperon population.

The net effect is an EoS that:
- Still allows hyperons to appear at moderate density (satisfying chemical equilibrium requirements).
- Becomes stiff enough at high density due to short-range repulsion to support stellar masses up to and beyond 2 M☉.

## Results

Using such repulsive hyperon-hyperon and hyperon-nucleon interactions in RMF or similar many-body frameworks, calculations show:

- Hyperons do appear in the stellar core (typically Λ hyperons first, at densities of order 2-3 times nuclear saturation density).
- Despite their presence, the resulting maximum mass configurations reach **≈ 2 solar masses**, matching observational constraints.
- The radius and other structural properties remain broadly consistent with astrophysical and nuclear constraints.

## Broader Implications

- The study demonstrates that the hyperon puzzle can be resolved **without excluding hyperons entirely**, contrary to some earlier proposals that avoided the problem by assuming hyperons simply don't appear (e.g., via extremely stiff nucleonic EoS alone or strong first-order phase transitions to quark matter before hyperon thresholds are reached).
- It emphasizes the importance of **three-body forces and multi-baryon repulsive interactions**, not just two-body potentials, in dense npeμ + hyperon matter.
- It highlights the necessity of future **hypernuclear experiments** (e.g., studies of Λ and Ξ hypernuclei, hyperon-nucleon scattering data) to better constrain these repulsive terms, since current experimental data at very high density (relevant for neutron star cores) is sparse and the extrapolation depends sensitively on the assumed model of short-range repulsion.

## Conclusion

By incorporating strong, short-range repulsive hyperonic interactions—motivated by vector meson exchange, three-body forces, or quark-level Pauli blocking—models can produce a nuclear equation of state that includes hyperons yet remains stiff enough at high density to support neutron stars with masses around 2 solar masses, thus offering a viable resolution to the long-standing hyperon puzzle in neutron star physics.

# Abstract

The hyperon puzzle refers to the tension between the theoretically expected softening of the neutron star equation of state (EOS) due to hyperon appearance at high densities and the observational constraint of two-solar-mass neutron stars. Once the central density of a neutron star exceeds several times nuclear saturation density, the nucleon chemical potential rises sufficiently to make the production of hyperons (particularly the Σ⁻ and Λ) energetically favorable. Since hyperons are more massive but carry lower Fermi pressure at fixed baryon density than nucleons, their onset acts as a new degree of freedom that softens the EOS, reducing the maximum mass supported against gravitational collapse—often to values well below 2 M☉, in conflict with precisely measured pulsar masses such as PSR J0348+0432 and PSR J0740+6620.

We show that this tension can be substantially relieved by incorporating strong short-range hyperon-nucleon and hyperon-hyperon repulsive core interactions, mediated by vector meson exchange (ω, φ) and multi-pomeron/quark-model-inspired repulsive terms, within a relativistic mean-field or Brueckner-Hartree-Fock framework. At short interparticle separations, the hard-core repulsion generates a steep rise in the hyperonic contribution to the pressure, counteracting the softening from the increased particle content. This additional repulsive pressure delays the softening of the EOS at high density, allowing the star to sustain the increased central pressure required for 2 M☉ configurations while still permitting hyperon population fractions consistent with hypernuclear experimental constraints (Λ binding energies, ΞN and ΣN scattering data). 

Our results demonstrate that a consistent treatment of short-distance hyperon repulsion—rather than the suppression of hyperon appearance altogether—provides a natural, microphysically motivated resolution to the hyperon puzzle, reconciling dense-matter microphysics with astrophysical mass-radius observations.

# Hard-Core Baryon-Baryon Interactions and 2 M☉ Neutron Stars

**Abstract**

The discovery of ~2 solar mass neutron stars poses a severe challenge to theoretical equations of state (EoS) that include hyperons, since the appearance of these strange baryons at densities of a few times nuclear saturation density typically softens the EoS considerably, often precluding stellar configurations massive enough to match observations—the well-known "hyperon puzzle." A key mechanism proposed to resolve this tension is the presence of strong short-range repulsive (hard-core) components in the baryon-baryon interaction, particularly in the hyperon-nucleon (YN) and hyperon-hyperon (YY) channels.

Realistic baryon-baryon potentials, derived from meson-exchange models, chiral effective field theory, or lattice QCD-inspired approaches, generically feature repulsive cores at short distances arising from vector meson exchange, quark Pauli-blocking effects, or other short-range dynamics. When incorporated into many-body calculations of dense hyperonic matter, these repulsive core contributions generate substantial additional pressure at high density, counteracting the softening effect caused by the onset of hyperonic degrees of freedom. This mechanism allows the EoS to remain sufficiently stiff even after hyperons populate the core, enabling maximum neutron star masses compatible with 2 M☉.

Microscopic calculations using Brueckner-Hartree-Fock, variational, and relativistic mean-field frameworks incorporating strongly repulsive hyperonic interactions—especially in the ΛΛ, ΣN, and ΞN channels—demonstrate that the stiffening from short-range repulsion can offset or even exceed the softening from hyperon admixture. This suggests that the hyperon puzzle need not require exotic solutions (e.g., strong three-body forces, phase transitions to quark matter, or modified gravity) if the underlying two-body hyperon-nucleon interactions possess sufficiently strong short-distance repulsion, consistent with emerging constraints from hypernuclear spectroscopy and (limited) hyperon-nucleon scattering data. Continued refinement of hyperonic interaction models, informed by both terrestrial experiments and astrophysical observations, remains essential to fully resolve the compatibility between hyperon-rich neutron star interiors and the observed maximum mass constraints.

# Abstract

The recent observations of massive neutron stars with masses ~2 M☉ have posed a significant challenge to theoretical models of dense matter equation of state (EOS), particularly those incorporating hyperonic degrees of freedom. The appearance of hyperons at densities beyond ~2-3 times nuclear saturation density typically softens the EOS considerably, leading to maximum masses well below the observational constraints—a discrepancy known as the "hyperon puzzle." In this work, we investigate the role of short-range, hard-core repulsive interactions among baryons in resolving this tension within the framework of relativistic mean-field (RMF) theory extended to include the full baryon octet.

We systematically incorporate additional repulsive contributions arising from vector meson exchange and multi-body (three- and four-body) force effects that become significant at high baryon density, effectively mimicking hard-core repulsion at short distances. These repulsive terms are calibrated to reproduce empirical hyperon-nucleon and hyperon-hyperon potential depths extracted from hypernuclear spectroscopy and femtoscopic correlation measurements from heavy-ion collisions, while remaining consistent with nuclear saturation properties and symmetry energy constraints.

Our results demonstrate that sufficiently strong hard-core repulsion among hyperons, particularly through enhanced vector coupling in the strangeness sector, can substantially stiffen the high-density EOS, allowing the maximum neutron star mass to reach or exceed 2 M☉ even with a sizable hyperon population. We explore the parameter space of hyperon coupling constants and repulsive core strengths, identifying the conditions under which hyperonic stars remain compatible with the M-R relations dictated by NICER measurements and tidal deformability constraints from gravitational wave observations (GW170817). We further examine the resulting composition, particle fractions, and adiabatic index profiles, showing that the onset of hyperons is delayed to higher densities and their fractional abundance is suppressed compared to standard hyperonic models lacking additional repulsion.

We conclude that hard-core repulsive interactions offer a viable and physically motivated mechanism to reconcile the presence of hyperons in dense stellar matter with the existence of massive neutron stars, without invoking exotic phase transitions or additional degrees of freedom. These findings underscore the importance of accurately constraining hyperonic interactions through upcoming hypernuclear experiments and multi-messenger astronomical observations to further refine the dense matter EOS.
